blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces Valiant's 1984 paper as a foundational work proposing a theory of learnability, analogous to computability but for what computers can learn rather than what they can compute. The paper seeks to define learnability in a general, algorithm-agnostic way, focusing on binary classification tasks where a learner must deduce a recognition algorithm from examples. Valiant formalizes this as 'probably approximately correct' (PAC) learning, where a learner must produce a hypothesis that approximates the target concept with high probability, using polynomial-time computations. Colyer highlights Valiant's abstract framework, which separates the learning protocol (e.g., querying examples or oracles) from the deduction procedure, and notes its relevance to both human learning and machine learning systems. The paper demonstrates learnability for classes like k-CNF and monotone DNF expressions, providing polynomial-time algorithms under specific conditions. Colyer underscores the paper's theoretical depth and its role in shaping modern machine learning theory.

A Theory of the Learnable

ABSTRACT: Humans appear to be able to learn new
concepts without needing to be programmed explicitly in
any conventional sense. In this paper we regard learning as
the phenomenon of knowledge acquisition in the absence of
explicit programming. We give a precise methodology for
studying this phenomenon from a computational viewpoint.
